/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
out=Path('tmp/pdfs')
out.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
parts=[]
print('pages',len(r.pages))
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
    t=p.extract_text()
    parts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n'+t)
    (out/f'page-{i}.txt').write_text(t)
(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(parts))
print(''.join(parts[:4]))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import math
from pypdf import PdfReader
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
for n,c,base in [(7,275,259),(8,900,820),(9,3011,2717),(10,10414,9124),(11,36368,31142)]:
    rate=math.log(c,4)/n
    hamming_ub=4**n/(1+3*n)
    print(f'n={n}: rate={rate:.6f}; gain={100*(rate-math.log(base,4)/n):.4f} percentage points; Hamming upper bound={hamming_ub:.1f}; redundancy gap={math.log2(hamming_ub/c):.4f} bits')
for p in [6,8]:
    for j,im in enumerate(r.pages[p].images):
        print('embedded image',p+1,j,im.name,im.image.size)
        im.image.save(f'tmp/pdfs/figure-page-{p+1}-{j}.png')
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: asymptotically efficient IDS codes can have poor rates at short lengths. Using learned embeddings to guide construction of explicit, reusable codebooks is a useful direction.

Algorithm 1 removes neighbors using exact Levenshtein distance. Consequently, the minimum-distance-three property follows independently of embedding accuracy, providing a sound basis for single-error correction with an exact decoder.

Table 1 demonstrates consistent improvements over random greedy selection across ten runs. At n=11, the best codebook contains 36,368 codewords versus 31,142 for random selection, a 16.8% cardinality improvement, corresponding to approximately one percentage point in code rate. The original-loss ablation also helps identify the revised loss's contribution.

The decoder reports zero failures in 10^8 random single-edit trials per tested length when checking four candidates. The source-code link, synthetic-data setup, and explicit acknowledgment of construction scalability and missing optimality proofs are useful.
weaknesses: The central density argument in Section 4.2 is mathematically unsupported: batch normalization does not make embeddings jointly Gaussian. Moreover, Gaussian point density is not established as a proxy for exact radius-two neighborhood size, particularly as the candidate set shrinks. The binary t-SNE visualization does not validate these assumptions. Direct correlations with neighborhood sizes and comparisons against conventional minimum-degree or lexicographic greedy selection are needed.

The headline combination of reliable correction and O(n) decoding is not established. The k=1 decoder fails on approximately 0.3–0.9% of trials, while the successful multi-candidate variant incurs O(n^2) verification according to Section 5.5. Logarithmic expected k-d-tree query time requires assumptions not established for these 64-dimensional embeddings. Figure 5 also shows k=1 runtime rising from 6 to 367 seconds between n=7 and n=11, providing no empirical demonstration of linear scaling. Zero sampled failures is encouraging but does not guarantee correction; exhaustive single-edit validation is feasible at these lengths.

The decoding comparison uses an unnecessarily weak baseline. Single-error decoding need not scan every codeword: enumerating possible edits with codebook hashing, or indexing precomputed single-edit neighborhoods, provides relevant exact alternatives with explicit memory tradeoffs. The general edit-distance hardness result does not establish hardness in this bounded-error setting. Without these comparisons, the practical value of neural decoding remains unclear.

The optimality and state-of-the-art claims exceed the evidence. Agreement with a chosen redundancy curve does not establish closeness to the optimum, and asymptotic redundancy expressions do not establish the best finite-length cardinalities of competing constructions. At n=11, even the elementary substitution sphere-packing bound leaves approximately a 3.4-fold cardinality gap above the reported codebook. Stronger finite-length search baselines and a closer comparison with related codebook-generation work [17] are needed.

The experiments establish performance on isolated segments containing one edit. The motivation concerns segmented streams and multiple errors, but boundary recovery, synchronization failures, and outer-code overhead are not evaluated. Thus, improvements in overall storage density or multiple-error correction remain un demonstrated.

Despite the repository link, the manuscript omits important reproducibility details: training-pair sampling, handling of variable-length inputs, convolution specifications, optimization settings, hardware, and construction time and peak memory. These omissions particularly limit assessment of the efficiency claims.
